children.translated_text: Homage to the blessed <s>Gaṇeśa</s> and to speech.
I bow to the pot-bellied one, great-bodied, with hanging lips and elephant ears,
the destroyer of obstacles, the son of <s>Pārvatī</s>, the leader of the hosts.
Apart from one who bears weapons, no one is accomplished in <s>Dhanurveda</s>.
Therefore, when night has arrived even in a dream, there should be reflection on the principle of <s>Śiva</s>.
Therefore the mind should not be placed in the swing of dull uncertainty.
In this treatise, the <s>Vīracintāmaṇi</s>, composed for those skilled in the bow, at certain points...
By whose practice, through grace, archers are perfected,
conquerors of hostile armies: that practice should be undertaken.
In whatever city even a single archer is famous,
from there enemies go far away, like deer from a lion's den.
The bow should be given by the teacher after examination by a Brahmin.

children.text: śaṭhe dhūrtte kṛtaghne ca mandabuddhau na dīyate ||
children.translated_text: It is not to be given to one who is deceitful, fraudulent, ungrateful, or dull-witted.

children.text: brāhmaṇāya dhanurdeyaṃ khaḍgaṃ vai kṣatriyāya ca
children.translated_text: The bow should be given to a Brahmin, and the sword to a Kshatriya.
One should have a spear given to a Vaishya, and a mace given to a Shudra.

children.text: dhanuścakraṃ tu kuntaṃ ca khaḍgaṃ ca churikāṃ gadām
children.translated_text: The bow, the discus, the spear, the sword, the dagger, and the mace,
and the seventh, arm-combat: thus the forms of combat are sevenfold.
A teacher is one skilled in the seven combats; a <s>Bhārgava</s> likewise in four.

children.text: dvābhyāṃ caiva bhavedyoddhā ekena gaṇako bhavet ||
children.translated_text: One skilled in two becomes a fighter, and one skilled in one becomes a reckoner.
<s>Hasta</s>, <s>Punarvasu</s>, <s>Puṣya</s>, <s>Rohiṇī</s>, and the three <s>Uttarā</s> constellations,
also <s>Anurādhā</s>, <s>Aśvinī</s>, <s>Revatī</s>, and the tenth lunar day,

children.text: janmasthe ca tṛtīye ca ṣaṣṭhe vai saptame tathā
children.translated_text: when the moon is in the natal sign, the third, the sixth, or the seventh,
or in the tenth or eleventh, one should have all rites performed.

children.text: tṛtīyā pañcamī caiva saptamī navamī tathā
children.translated_text: The third, fifth, seventh, and ninth lunar days,

children.text: trayodaśī dvādaśī ca tithayaśca śubhā matāḥ ||
children.translated_text: and the thirteenth and twelfth lunar days are regarded as auspicious dates.
Sunday, Friday, and Thursday as well,
these three weekdays are fortunate for beginning work with weapons.
On these days the teacher should have weapons given to the pupil,
after satisfying the gods with gifts and oblations according to scriptural rule.
There he should feed Brahmins and many maidens too.
He should reverently honor ascetics, and others who are yogins of <s>Śiva</s>.
With food and drink and the like, with garments, ornaments, and adornments,
and with varied perfumes and garlands, he should worship the teacher there.
The pupil, having fasted and assuming a reverent posture,
should join his hands there and request the bow from the teacher.

children.text: aṅganyāsas tataḥ kāryaḥ śivoktaḥ siddhim icchatā
children.translated_text: Then a placing of the deities on the limbs, taught by <s>Śiva</s>, should be performed by one desiring success,
by the teacher for the pupil, destroying sin and removing obstacles.
He should place <s>Īśa</s> at the place of the topknot, and <s>Keśava</s> on the pair of arms,
<s>Brahmā</s> in the middle of the navel, and the lord of hosts on the thighs.
The mantra in the limb-placing is:
Oṃ hauṃ, homage to <s>Śaṅkara</s> in the middle of the topknot.
Oṃ hauṃ, homage to <s>Keśava</s> on the two arms.
Oṃ hauṃ, homage to <s>Brahmā</s> in the middle of the navel.
Oṃ hauṃ, homage to <s>Gaṇapati</s> on the two thighs.
He should perform such a nyāsa (ritual placement), by which welfare will arise.
Other evil beings also never do harm.
To the pupil he should give a human bow, consecrated with the mantras of <s>Dhanurveda</s>,
with the mantra beginning 'from joint to joint,' according to the Vedic rule.
First he should have him pierce a flower with an arrow that has no iron head.
Then, with one furnished with a head, he should have him pierce a fish.
After that he should perform the piercing of flesh; thus the piercing is threefold.

children.text: pūrvavedhaiḥ kṛtāḥ puṃsā śarāḥ syuḥ sarvasādhakāḥ ||
children.translated_text: Arrows used by a man in the former piercings become effective for every purpose.
And in the piercing, when the arrow has been drawn in this way and falls,
if it resorts to the eastern quarter, he will always be victorious and happy.
In the south there is terrible quarrel and then a journey to a foreign land.

children.text: paścime dhanadhānyaṃ ca sarvaṃ caivottare bhavet ||
children.translated_text: In the west there are wealth and grain, and in the north everything desirable.
A fall in the northeast is bad, but the other intermediate directions are auspicious,
promoting every prosperity and granting success in work with weapons.
Having performed the threefold piercing in this way, to the sounds of conches and kettledrums,
then, after bowing to the teacher, he should present the bow and arrows.
The first bow is the personal bow; the second is the battle bow.
It is auspicious when it measures slightly less than the strength of one's own arms.

children.text: varaṃ prāṇādhiko dhanvī natu prāṇādhikaṃ dhanuḥ
children.translated_text: Better an archer stronger than his bow than a bow stronger than the archer,

children.text: dhanuṣā pīḍyamānastu dhanvī lakṣyaṃ na paśyati ||
children.translated_text: for an archer oppressed by his bow does not see the target.
Therefore a bow measured by one's own strength is productive of good fortune.

children.text: devānāmuttamaṃ cāpaṃ tato nyūnaṃ ca mānavam ||
children.translated_text: The bow of the gods is supreme; below that is the human bow.
A bow of five and a half hastas is declared the best bow.

children.text: tad vijñeyaṃ dhanur divyaṃ śaṅkareṇa dhṛtaṃ purā ||
children.translated_text: That should be known as the divine bow once borne by <s>Śaṅkara</s>.
After him it was held by <s>Paraśurāma</s>, then by the wise <s>Droṇa</s>.
From <s>Droṇa</s> it was taken by <s>Pārtha</s>, and then held by <s>Sātyaki</s>.
In the <s>Kṛta</s> age <s>Mahādeva</s>, in the <s>Tretā</s> age <s>Bhārgava</s>,
and in the <s>Dvāpara</s> age the Brahmin <s>Droṇa</s> bore the divine bow.
A hasta is twenty-four aṅgulas; a bow of four hastas
is the human bow, endowed with all proper marks.

children.text: triparvaṃ pañcaparvaṃ ca saptaparvaṃ ca kīrtitam
children.translated_text: A bow of three joints, five joints, and seven joints is taught,
and a nine-jointed <s>kodaṇḍa</s> as well: these four kinds bestow good fortune.

children.text: catuḥparvaṃ ca ṣaṭparvam aṣṭaparvaṃ ca varjayet
children.translated_text: One should avoid bows of four joints, six joints, and eight joints.
For some, the bow may measure nine spans.

children.text: atijīrṇam apakvaṃ ca jñātidhṛṣṭaṃ tathaiva ca
children.translated_text: One that is excessively old, unripe, or rubbed by kinsmen, likewise
burnt, cut, or having an outer or inner hand-defect, should not be made.
One lacking a string, overstrained by the string, or joined with defects of the shaft,

children.text: galagranthi talagranthi na kartavyaṃ sadā budhaiḥ ||
children.translated_text: with a knot at the neck or a knot at the base, should never be made by the wise.
An unripe one breaks; an excessively old one is harsh.

children.text: jñātidhṛṣṭaṃ tu sodvegaṃ kalaho bāndhavaiḥ saha ||
children.translated_text: One rubbed by kinsmen is troublesome, bringing quarrel with relatives.
By a burnt one the house is burned; a perforated one destroys intelligence.

children.text: bāhye lakṣyaṃ na labhyeta tathaivābhyantare'pi ca ||
children.translated_text: With an external defect the target is not reached, and likewise with an internal one.

children.text: hīne tu saṃdhite bāṇe saṃgrāme bhaṅgakārakam
children.translated_text: When an inferior arrow is fitted, it causes breaking in battle.

children.text: ākrānte tu punarlakṣye lakṣyaṃ na prāpyate dṛḍham ||
children.translated_text: But when the bow is overstrained, the target is not firmly reached at the mark.
A bow with a neck-knot or base-knot causes loss of wealth.
Free from these defects, it produces all the proper marks.

children.text: śārṅgaṃ tu vai dhanurdivyaṃ tadviṣṇoḥ paramāyudham
children.translated_text: The <s>Śārṅga</s> bow is divine; it is the supreme weapon of <s>Viṣṇu</s>.
Its measure is seven spans, and it was fashioned by <s>Viśvakarman</s>.

children.text: na svarge na ca pātāle na bhūmau kasyacitkare
children.translated_text: Neither in heaven, nor in the netherworld, nor on earth is it in anyone’s hand;
that bow does not come under control, except for the one <s>Puruṣottama</s>.

children.text: pauruṣeyaṃ tu yat kāryaṃ bahuyatnena yojitam
children.translated_text: But the human-made bow that is to be made should be joined with great effort.
Measured by seven spans, it accomplishes every purpose.

children.text: prāyo jñeyaṃ dhanuḥ śārṅgaṃ gajārohasya sādhanam
children.translated_text: The <s>Śārṅga</s> bow is generally to be known as the equipment of one mounted on an elephant;

children.text: rathināṃ ca padātīnāṃ vāṃśaṃ cāpaṃ prakīrtitam ||
children.translated_text: and for chariot-warriors and foot-soldiers the bamboo bow is proclaimed.
I shall state the characteristics of strings, and what kind of string one should make.
It should be of the measure of the bow, without joints, made with triple-stranded threads.

children.text: vartitaḥ syād guṇaḥ sūkṣmaḥ sarvakāryasaho yudhi
children.translated_text: The string should be twisted, fine, and able to endure every task in battle.
A string should be made from silk threads, measured to the size of the little finger.
In the absence of silk thread, the sinew of a deer is desired.
For the sake of a bowstring, the sinews of buffaloes or cows are then to be collected.
Or the hide of a cow slain at that time, or of a goat,
one may make into an excellent string in the form of reverse-running fibers.
A string may be made from the bark of mature bamboo, firm and strong.
Bound with silk thread, it endures every task in battle.
When the month of <s>Bhādrapada</s> has arrived, the bark of the arka plant is praised.

children.text: tasyāstatra guṇaḥ kāryaḥ pavitraḥ sthāvaro dṛḍhaḥ ||
children.translated_text: From it a string should then be made, pure, stable, and firm.
Eighteen hands are remembered for the rounded threads of arka fiber.

children.text: tadvṛttaṃ triguṇaṃ kāryaṃ pramāṇo'yaṃ guṇasya ca ||
children.translated_text: That round cord should be made threefold; this too is the measure of the string.
The arrowhead should be of pure iron, sharp-edged, and sharp-pointed.
One should attach it with diamond-cement, according to the strength of the shaft and feathers.
The <s>ārāmukha</s>, the razor-edged <s>kṣurapra</s>, the cow-tail shape, and the half-moon,

children.text: sūcīmukhaṃ ca bhallaṃ ca vatsadantaṃ suvallabham ||
children.translated_text: the needle-point, the <s>bhalla</s>, the calf-tooth, and the very dear one,
the barbed <s>karṇika</s>, the crow-beak, and many others as well:
arrowheads in various regions exist in many forms.
With the <s>ārāmukha</s> one should pierce leather, and with the <s>kṣurapra</s> a bow;
with the needle-point, armor; with the half-moon, the head.

children.text: bhallena hṛdayaṃ vedhyaṃ dvibhallena tathaiva ca
children.translated_text: The heart is to be pierced with the <s>bhalla</s>, and likewise with the double-<s>bhalla</s>.

children.text: lohaṃ ca kākatuṇḍena lakṣyaṃ gopucchakena ca ||
children.translated_text: Iron is pierced with the crow-beak, and a target with the cow-tail head.
Another cow-tail head is to be known, made of pure bronze.
By its mouth and also by its neck, the penetration is measured by a finger’s breadth.
I shall explain the tempering of an arrowhead, the application of divine herbs,
by which one may split armors hard to pierce as if they were leaves of a tree.

children.text: pippalī saindhavaṃ kuṣṭhaṃ gomūtreṇa ca peṣayet
children.translated_text: One should grind long pepper, rock salt, and kuṣṭha with cow urine.
With this one should smear the weapon; when smeared, one should heat it in fire.
The herb, not causing poisonous discharge, strongly applied, and heated in fire,

children.text: tato nirvāpitaṃ lohaṃ tatra vedhe viśiṣyate ||
children.translated_text: then the iron quenched in it becomes excellent in penetration.
Ground with the five salts, with beeswax and mustard seeds,
with these one should coat the weapon; when coated, one should heat it in fire.
When its heated head has the color like the neck of a peacock, through that herb,
then it is to be known as stainless; one should temper the excellent weapon.
Those arrows that are wholly of iron are proclaimed to be <s>nārāca</s> arrows.
Furnished with five broad feathers, they sometimes become effective.
Tubular arrows are light arrows, propelled by a tube-machine.

children.text: yujyante dūrapāteṣu durge yuddheṣu te matāḥ ||
children.translated_text: They are used for long-distance shots and are considered suitable in battles at forts.
Eight positions are to be prescribed; one should employ them according to different tasks.

children.text: sṛṣṭyaḥ pañca samākhyātā vyāyāḥ pañca prakīrtitāḥ ||
children.translated_text: Five releases are declared, and five extensions are proclaimed.
With the left foot in front and the right knee bent,

children.text: ālīḍhe tu prakartakaṃ tathā caivānu kuñcitam ||
children.translated_text: in the <s>ālīḍha</s> posture the cutting action is to be done, and likewise it is bent afterward.
But with the right foot placed in front, it is especially good for a distant shot.

children.text: pādau na vistarau kāryau samau hastapramāṇataḥ ||
children.translated_text: The feet should not be set wide apart; they should be even, at the measure of a hand.
A special stance is to be known for piercing a concealed target.

children.text: same pāte samau pādau niṣkampaṃ ca susaṃgatau ||
children.translated_text: For an even shot the two feet are even, unmoving and well joined.

children.text: asame ca purobhāge hastamātreṇa taṃ viduḥ
children.translated_text: For an uneven one, they know the forward part to be by the measure of a hand.
There the two thighs are contracted, with the knees gone down to the ground.
Standing on broken or uneven ground is a posture for firm piercing.
The left knee is placed on the ground, and the right is well bent.

children.text: savyaṃ jānu nataṃ bhūmau dakṣiṇaṃ na ca kuñcitam
children.translated_text: Where the left knee is bent down to the ground and the right is not bent,

children.text: agrato yatra dātavyaṃ taṃ vidyād garuḍaṃ kramam ||
children.translated_text: where something is to be given forward, one should know that as the <s>garuḍa</s> sequence.
The lotus-seat is well known; having sat down, in due order,
Here the auspiciously marked standing posture of archers is to be known.
Patākā, guṇamuṣṭi, and likewise siṃhakarṇa,
matsarī, kākatuṇḍī, and yojanīyā are to be applied in due order.
Where the forefinger is long and rests at the root of the thumb,

children.text: patākā sā ca vijñeyā nālikā dūramokṣaṇe ||
children.translated_text: that is to be known as patākā, for shooting a nālikā at a distance.
If the thumb enters between the forefinger and middle finger,
that is known as guṇamuṣṭi, for releasing thick nārācas.
When the tip of the forefinger is well placed at the middle part of the thumb,
that is to be known as siṃhakarṇa, for piercing a firm target.
When the tip of the forefinger is well set at the root of the thumbnail,

children.text: matsarī sā ca vijñeyā sūkṣmalakṣyasya bhedane ||
children.translated_text: that is to be known as matsarī, for splitting a subtle target.

children.text: aṅguṣṭhāgre tu tarjanyā mukhaṃ yatra niveśitam
children.translated_text: Where the face of the forefinger is placed at the tip of the thumb,

children.text: kākatuṇḍī ca sā jñeyā sthūlalakṣyeṣu yojitā ||
children.translated_text: that is known as kākatuṇḍī, employed for large targets.

children.text: sandhānaṃ trividhaṃ proktam adha ūrdhvaṃ samaṃ yadā
children.translated_text: Nocking is said to be threefold: low, high, and level.
One should apply the three methods in tasks according to their order.
For an extremely long fall or range, a level target is certain;
one should make a firm strike when a high nocking is applied.

children.text: kaiśikaḥ śaramūle ca śaraśūṅge ca sāttvikaḥ
children.translated_text: Kaiśika is at the base of the arrow, sāttvika at the arrow-tip,
vatsakarṇa at the ear, and bharata should be at the neck.

children.text: aṃsake skandhanāmā ca vyāyāḥ pañca prakīrtitāḥ
children.translated_text: At the shoulder is the one named skandha; five vyāyas are proclaimed.
Kaiśika is for varied combat, and sāttvika for low targets.
Vatsakarṇa is to be known for use, and bharata for firm piercing.

children.text: dṛḍhabhede ca dūre ca skandhanāmānam uddiśet ||
children.translated_text: For firm piercing and at a distance, one should prescribe the one named skandha.

children.text: lakṣyaṃ caturvidhaṃ jñeyaṃ sthiraṃ caiva calaṃ tathā
children.translated_text: A target is to be known as fourfold: stationary, moving,
moving-and-stationary, and both-moving; these are the distinctions in order.

children.text: ātmānaṃ susthiraṃ kṛtvā lakṣyaṃ caiva sthiraṃ budhaḥ
children.translated_text: Having made himself very steady, and the target also steady, the wise man

children.text: vedhayet triprakāraṃ tu sthiravedhī sa ucyate ||
children.translated_text: should pierce it in the threefold manner; he is called a stationary-shot archer.
But one who pierces a moving target while himself standing steady

children.text: calavedhīti sa prokta ācāryeṇa śivena vai ||
children.translated_text: is called a moving-shot archer by the teacher <s>Śiva</s>.

children.text: dhanvī tu calate yatra sthiralakṣye samāhitaḥ
children.translated_text: Where the archer moves while intent upon a stationary target,
there it becomes moving-and-stationary; it is declared to be self-measured.

children.text: ubhāveva calau yatra lakṣyaṃ vāpi dhanurdharaḥ
children.translated_text: Where both are moving, the target or else the bowman,

children.text: tad vijñeyaṃ dvayacalaṃ śrameṇaiva hi sādhakaḥ ||
children.translated_text: that is to be known as both-moving; it is accomplished only through exertion.
By exertion an unmoving target, a distant one, and repeated piercing are attained;
by exertion the hard fist quickly brings accomplishment.
By exertion comes skill in varied piercing; by exertion victory is obtained.

children.text: tasmād gurusamīpe tu śramaḥ kāryo vijānatā ||
children.translated_text: Therefore an informed man should exert himself in the presence of the guru.

children.text: prathamaṃ vāmahastena yaḥ śramaṃ kurute naraḥ
children.translated_text: The man who first practices exertion with the left hand,
for him success in bow-work arises very quickly.
When the left hand has been perfected, afterward he should begin with the right.
He should practice with both hands, with nārācas and likewise with arrows.

children.text: vāmenaiva śramaṃ kuryāt susiddhe dakṣiṇe kare
children.translated_text: He should practice with the left hand alone when the right hand is well perfected,

children.text: viśākhasthānake caiva tathā vyāye ca kaiśike ||
children.translated_text: and also in the viśākha stance and in the kaiśika vyāya.
When the sun has risen, he should set the target in the west;
in the afternoon the target should be placed toward the eastern quarter.
It should always be done to the north; the obstructing position is praised.

children.text: saṃgrāmeṇa vinā kāryaṃ na lakṣyaṃ dakṣiṇāmukham ||
children.translated_text: Except in battle, a target should not be made south-facing.
A target at an interval of sixty kāṇḍas is proclaimed the highest target;
forty is middling, and twenty is the lowest.
This has been stated for arrows; now listen concerning nārācas.
For nārācas, forty and sixteen are then to be the measure.

children.text: catuḥśataiśca kāṇḍānāṃ yo hi lakṣyaṃ samabhyaset
children.translated_text: He who practices at the target with four hundred shafts

children.text: sūryodaye cāstakāle sa jyeṣṭho dhanvināṃ bhavet ||
children.translated_text: at sunrise and at sunset becomes the foremost of archers.
With three hundred he is middling, and with two hundred the lowest.
One should make the target the height of a man and furnished with a circular mark.
One who pierces above is best, one who pierces at the navel is middling,

children.text: yaḥ pādavedhī lakṣyasya sa kaniṣṭhatamo bhavet ||
children.translated_text: and one who pierces the foot of the target is the very lowest.

children.text: ataḥ paraṃ pravakṣyāmi śarāṇāṃ lakṣaṇaṃ śubham
children.translated_text: After this I shall explain the auspicious characteristics of arrows:
one should reject such an arrow as is thick, excessively fine, born from unripe or overripe ground,

children.text: ādravaṃ yad viśīrṇaṃ ca varjayed īdṛśaṃ śaram
children.translated_text: moist, or split apart.
One should take a hard, round shaft that is full-jointed, well matured, pale, and gathered at the proper time,
and that comes from a good region.

children.text: dvau hastau muṣṭihīnau ca dairghye sthaulye kaniṣṭhikāḥ ||
children.translated_text: In length it should be two hastas less a fist, and in thickness like the little finger.
These are to be prescribed as the measure of an arrow; then one should draw it by the circular grip.
The feathers of herons, geese, hawks, fish-eaters, krauñcas, cuckoos,

children.text: gṛdhrāṇāṃ ca kuraṅgānāṃ pakṣā eteṣu śobhanāḥ ||
children.translated_text: vultures, and antelopes are good for these.
For a single arrow one should make four feathers.
One should not make a division of feathers measuring six aṅgulas.
Feathers measured at ten aṅgulas are for the missile of a śārṅga bow.
Four in number, firm, and fastened with sinew threads, they should be fitted.
Arrows are to be known as threefold: female, male, and neuter.
One that is thick in front is female; one thick behind is male.
One that is even is to be known as neuter; it is praised for the purpose of the target.
The female has long flight, while the male is firm in piercing.
The neuter arrow is a target-piercer: so they know the characteristics of arrows.

children.text: aṣṭamī ca tathāmā ca varjanīyā caturdaśī
children.translated_text: The eighth lunar day, likewise the new-moon day, and the fourteenth are to be avoided,
and the full-moon day too, for the whole day, one should avoid in bow-work.

children.text: akālagarjito devo durdinaṃ vā yadā bhavet
children.translated_text: When the god thunders out of season, or when there is bad weather,
or when the target has been struck in its front section, they declare a suspension of study.

children.text: śramaṃ ca kurvato yatra bhujaṅgo yadi dṛśyate
children.translated_text: Where, while one is doing exertion-practice, a snake is seen,
or when the bow breaks during the very act of exertion-practice,

children.text: truṭyate vā guṇo yatra prathame bāṇamokṣaṇe
children.translated_text: or where the string snaps at the first release of the arrow,

children.text: śramaṃ tatra na kurvīta śastre matimatāṃ varaḥ ||
children.translated_text: there one should not practice exertion, O best of the wise in arms.
I shall explain the procedural operations, famous and to be accomplished by exertion,
by the mere knowledge of which success comes, and not otherwise.
First, having strung the bow, he should then wrap the <s>tūlikā</s>;

children.text: sthānakaṃ tu tataḥ kuryād bāṇopari karaṃ nyaset ||
children.translated_text: then he should assume the stance and place the hand upon the arrow.
The weighing and steadiness of the bow should be done with the left hand;

children.text: ādānaṃ tu tataḥ kṛtvā sandhānaṃ tu tataḥ param ||
children.translated_text: then, after making the taking-up, next comes the fitting of the arrow.
Having drawn the bow from the target, he should not cause it to strike the ground.
In battle they should bow to <s>Śiva</s>, to the lord of obstacles, and to the excellent guru.
The guru's permission is to be requested for drawing the arrow.
With effort he should fill the vital breath together with the arrow.
Having drawn it with breath-retention, he should release it with the sound <s>huṃ</s>.
Thus this practice procedure is to be performed by an archer who desires success.

children.text: ṣaṇmāsāt sidhyate muṣṭiḥ śarāḥ saṃvatsareṇa tu
children.translated_text: The grip is perfected in six months, and arrows in a year;
the <s>nārācas</s> are perfected for him with whom <s>Maheśvara</s> is pleased.
He should hold the arrow like a flower and press the bow like a snake;
he should think of the target as wealth, if he desires success for himself.
Teachers desire technique, the <s>Bhārgavas</s> desire distance;

children.text: rājāno dṛṣṭim icchanti lakṣyam icchanti cetare ||
children.translated_text: kings desire sight, and others desire the target.
Since the pleasing of people arises from striking the target,
therefore piercing the target is praised even with an inferior arrow.
Standing in the <s>viśākha</s> stance, he should perform an even fitting of the arrow,
with a cow-tail-faced arrow and with a lion-ear grip.
He should draw in the <s>kaiśika-vyāya</s>, and then shake the topknot.

children.text: pūrvāparau samau kāryau samāṃsau niścalau karau ||
children.translated_text: The front and back should be made even; both arms should be even and motionless.
He should not blink the eyes; he should fix his gaze on the target.
He should set the target, covered by the grip, at the point of the arrow.
Having conceived the mind as situated in the grip, he should then release the shaft.

children.text: sa ca lakṣyeṣu kartavyo lakṣye yodho jitaśramaḥ ||
children.translated_text: And this is to be done among targets by a warrior whose exertion has been mastered.

children.text: ādānaṃ caiva tūṇīrāt sandhānaṃ karṣaṇaṃ tathā
children.translated_text: Taking the arrow from the quiver, fitting it, drawing it,

children.text: kṣepaṇaṃ ca tvarāyukto bāṇasya kurute tu yaḥ ||
children.translated_text: and releasing it: he who performs the arrow's action with speed,
for him, through constant practice, quick accomplishment comes about.
When the <s>pratyālīḍha</s> stance has been made, he should perform a downward fitting.
With the banner-shaped grip, a female arrow is one that falls far.
Having approached like a frog, he should perform an upward fitting.

children.text: skandhavyāyena vajrasya muṣṭyā puṃmārgaṇe na ca
children.translated_text: With the shoulder exertion, and with the thunderbolt grip, not on the male arrow;
an extreme gracefulness of the arms and firm piercing power arise.
Needle-pointed, fish-tailed, and the third, whirling like a bee:
these three praised courses of arrows have been taught by the wise.
The needle-pointed course arises for that arrow
when the feather is to be observed, or when it has deficient feathering.

children.text: karkaśe na tu cāpena yat kṛṣyeddhīnamuṣṭinā
children.translated_text: When one draws with a rough bow and with an inferior grip,
the fish-tailed course of that arrow is proclaimed.
This whirling course like a bee has indeed been taught by good men in exertion-practice;

children.text: ṛjutve na vinā yāti kṣepyamānastu sāyakaḥ ||
children.translated_text: when being shot, the arrow does not go without straightness.
Going left, going right, going upward, and going downward:
four courses are stated as causes of an arrow's deflection.
When the string-grip trembles behind the arrow,
and the bow-grip faces forward, then its course will be to the left.
For one whose grasp is slack and devoid of straightness,

children.text: pārśve tu dakṣiṇaṃ yāti sāyakasya na saṃśayaḥ ||
children.translated_text: the arrow goes to the right side; there is no doubt.
If the bow-grip is above and the string-grip is below,

children.text: samukto mārgaṇo lakṣyādūrdhvaṃ yāti na saṃśayaḥ ||
children.translated_text: the released arrow goes above the target; there is no doubt.

children.text: ākarṣaṇe caiva bāṇasya cāpe muṣṭiradho bhavet
children.translated_text: And if, in drawing the arrow on the bow, the grip is below,
and the string-grip is above, then its course goes downward.
When there is conjunction of the target, the arrow-point, and the gaze,

children.text: tadānīm ujjhito bāṇo lakṣyānna calati dhruvam ||
children.translated_text: then the released arrow surely does not move away from the target.
Faultless, soundless, and released by the two even grips,
the arrow pierces things that are hard to pierce; of this there is no doubt.
An arrow that is drawn, sharpened, purified, and firmly released

children.text: naro nāgāśca kāyeṣu na sa tiṣṭhati mārgaṇaḥ ||
children.translated_text: does not remain in the bodies of men or elephants.

children.text: yasya tṛṇasamā bāṇā yat saṃdhānasamaṃ dhanuḥ
children.translated_text: He whose arrows are like grass, whose bow is equal to the fitting,

children.text: yasya prāṇasamā maurvī sa dhanvī dhanvināṃ varaḥ ||
children.translated_text: and whose bowstring is like his own breath, that archer is the best of archers.
Iron, hide, a pot, and a lump of clay: these four

children.text: yo bhinatti na tasyeṣur vajriṇāpi ca bādhyate ||
children.translated_text: if one pierces them, his arrow is not obstructed even by the wielder of the thunderbolt.
He should have iron plates made to the measure of one and a half aṅgulas.
Having pierced them with a single arrow, a man becomes one who strikes firmly.
The man who pierces twenty-four hides with an arrow

children.text: tasya bāṇo gajendrasya kāyaṃ nirbhidya gacchati ||
children.translated_text: Its arrow passes through the body of the lordly elephant.

children.text: bhrāmyajjale ghaṭo vedhyaḥ cakre mṛtpiṇḍakaṃ tathā
children.translated_text: A pot in whirling water should be pierced, and likewise a clay lump on a wheel.
Whoever can split it while it is revolving is called a hard-piercing archer.
Iron should be pierced with the crow-beak head, and hide with the cāra point.

children.text: mṛtpiṇḍaṃ ca ghaṭaṃ caiva vidhyetsūcīmukhena vai ||
children.translated_text: A clay lump and also a pot should indeed be pierced with the needle-point head.
The turning that breaks arrows, and also the cutting of wood,

children.text: bindukaṃ caiva yugakaṃ yo vetti sa jayī bhavet ||
children.translated_text: the binduka and the yugaka: he who knows these becomes victorious.
One should cut, head-on, the shaft held at the place of the target,
after making one's own fist somewhat ready, with a two-edged arrow moving crosswise.

children.text: saṃmukhaṃ bāṇam āyāntaṃ tiryagbāṇaṃ na saṃcaret
children.translated_text: When an arrow is coming directly toward him, the crosswise arrow should not miss its course.

children.text: prāptaṃ śareṇa yaśchindyād bāṇacchedī sa ucyate ||
children.translated_text: He who cuts the arriving arrow with an arrow is called an arrow-cutter.
Having fastened a horsehair to a piece of wood and tied a cowrie shell there,

children.text: hastena bhrāmyamāṇaṃ ca yo hanti sa dhanurdharaḥ ||
children.translated_text: he who strikes it as it is being whirled by the hand is an archer.
One should set the weapon in fivefold fashion, pure and like a bandhuka flower.

children.text: hāstikaṃ bindukaṃ yastu citrabhedī sa ucyate ||
children.translated_text: He who knows the elephant-shot and the binduka is called a variegated-piercing archer.

children.text: lakṣyaviddhaṃ kāṣṭhaṃ kṣipraṃ dūramūrūrddha vapuḥ sthitam
children.translated_text: A piece of wood that has been pierced as a target, standing with its body far off, high, and swift,
with an arrow coming by itself to the back, with the upturned tail-end as its face,
he who strikes it with a pair of arrows through the discipline of rapid fitting to the bowstring,
he is the best among bowmen, honored by all kings.
At the target-place one should set a fresh piece of wood resembling a cow's tail.

children.text: yaḥ chindyāttaṃ kṣurapreṇa kāṣṭhavedhī sa yāyate ||
children.translated_text: He who cuts it with a razor-headed arrow is known as a wood-piercer.
At the target-place one should set a bronze vessel at a distance of two hastas.
One should strike it with pebbles; when a sound arises,

children.text: yatropalabhyate śabdaḥ samyak taṃ tatra cintayet
children.translated_text: wherever the sound is perceived, he should fix his thought correctly there.
Through concentration of the organs of action and the mind, he should bring the target to certainty.
Again, for the sake of producing sound, he should strike what has been split with a pebble.

children.text: tato bāṇena taṃ hanyāt tadavadhānena dhīmatā
children.translated_text: Then the wise man should strike it with an arrow, with attention fixed on that.

children.text: etacca duṣkaraṃ karma bhāgyāt kasyāpi sidhyati ||
children.translated_text: This is a difficult feat, and it succeeds for some man only by good fortune.

children.text: atha śramavidhiṃ kuryād yāvat siddhiḥ prajāyate
children.translated_text: Next he should perform the rule of exertion until success is produced.

children.text: śrame siddhe ca varṣāsu naiva grāhyaṃ dhanuṣkare ||
children.translated_text: And when exertion has been mastered, during the rains the bow-work should not be taken up.
For the sake of not forgetting the previous practice of weapons,

children.text: māsadvayaṃ śramaṃ kuryāt prati varṣaṃ śaradṛtau ||
children.translated_text: he should practice exertion for two months every year in the autumn season.

children.text: jāte cāśvayuje māsi navamī devatā dine
children.translated_text: When the month of <s>Āśvayuja</s> has come, on the ninth day, the day sacred to the deity,

children.text: pūjayed īśvarīṃ caṇḍīṃ guruṃ śāstrāṇi vājigaḥ ||
children.translated_text: he should worship the goddess <s>Caṇḍī</s>, the guru, the treatises, and the horses.
He should give fees to brahmins and then worship maidens.
He should offer an animal sacrifice to the goddess, with auspicious song and instrumental music.

children.text: śūlena pāhi no devi pāhi khaḍgeṇa cāmbike
children.translated_text: Protect us with the spear, O goddess; protect us with the sword, O <s>Ambikā</s>.
Protect us with the sound of the bell and with the sound of the bowstring.

children.text: prācyāṃ rakṣa pratīcyāṃ ca caṇḍike rakṣa dakṣiṇe
children.translated_text: Guard the east and the west, O <s>Caṇḍikā</s>; guard the south.
And in the north, O Lady, guard by the whirling of your own spear.

children.text: saumyāni yāni rūpāṇi trailokye vicaranti te
children.translated_text: Whatever gentle forms of yours move about in the three worlds,

children.text: yāni cātyarthaghorāṇi tai rakṣāsmān tathā bhuvam ||
children.translated_text: and whatever are exceedingly terrible, by those protect us and likewise the earth.
After that he should accomplish the mantras taught in the Veda and stated in the Āgamas,
for the success of the operations of the astras, by the rules of recitation and oblation.
The Brahma, Nārāyaṇa, Śaiva, Aindra, Vāyavya, Vāruṇa,
and Āgneya astras also, given by the guru, he should master.
A man who has obtained astras should be pure, pervaded by mind, speech, and action.
Astra-weapons burn a man who is an unfit vessel and incapable.

children.text: prayogaṃ copasaṃhāraṃ yo vetti sa dhanurdharaḥ
children.translated_text: He who knows their deployment and withdrawal is an archer.
A wise man should never employ astras in an ordinary action.
Having taken lāṅgalī tuber under the Hasta asterism, by smearing it,

children.text: śūrasyāpi raṇe puṃso darpaṃ harati tatkṣaṇāt ||
children.translated_text: it at once removes the pride even of a brave man in battle.
Having taken the root of apāmārga under auspicious yoga-asterisms,
by mere application it wards off all weapons of heroes.
Adhaḥpuṣpī, śaṅkhapuṣpī, lajjālu, girikarṇikā,
nīlinī and sahadevī, and likewise the leaves of muñja and arka,

children.text: viṣṇukrāntā ca sarvāsāṃ jaṭā grāhyā raverdine
children.translated_text: and viṣṇukrāntā: the roots of all these are to be taken on a Sunday.

children.text: baddhvā bhuje vilepād vā kāye sarvāstrāpavārakaḥ ||
children.translated_text: When bound on the arm or smeared on the body, it wards off all astras.
For him there arises no fear of all beasts such as tigers, nor of beings such as spirits,
nor fear from animals; the eight Mothers are in his body.
Powder taken under the Hasta asterism should be from the musk-rat.
By its power, an elephant certainly comes face to face with men.
Smearing the limbs with powder of musk-rat and śrīphala,
an extremely rut-maddened elephant, smelling the scent, gives up its rut.
With the root dug up under Puṣya and Sunday and placed in the mouth together with betel-nut,

children.text: dehaṃ sphuṭati notīkṣṇaṃ maṇḍalāgre raṇe nṝṇām ||
children.translated_text: the body of men in battle does not split even before a sharp circular edge.
The northern root of gāmbhārī, brought before the mouth,
when ritually extracted under Puṣya and Sunday, wards off there a mass of weapons.

children.text: śubhrāyāḥ śarapuṅkhāyā jaṭā nīlī jaṭā tathā
children.translated_text: The root of white śarapuṅkhā and likewise the root of nīlī,

children.text: bhuje śirasi vaktre vā sthitā śastranivārikā ||
children.translated_text: placed on the arm, head, or face, wards off weapons.
It destroys fear of spirits, snakes, and thieves when taken under Puṣya and Sunday.
First a bath is performed; he should be covered with white garments.
Having worshiped the weapons also, he should then recite the protection mantra
over the general, the elephant-riders, the horsemen, and all around.
He should clothe the chiefs and the others also with wealth and garments.

children.text: pūrvaṃ sārathimāropya rathe sajjet tataḥ svayam ||
children.translated_text: Having first mounted the charioteer, he should equip himself on the chariot thereafter.
He should fill the quiver with four hundred arrows.

children.text: śaṅkhaṃ cakraṃ gadāṃ śaktiṃ mudgaraṃ parighaṃ tathā ||
children.translated_text: He should set down a conch, discus, mace, spear, club, and iron bar as well,
a nārāca arrow, axe, lance, paṭṭiśa, and the like.
He himself should mount for battle from the position of men and the eight elephants.
With one quiver fastened at his waist, bearing sword, spear, and bow,
then he should recite the names of <s>Arjuna</s>, preceded by remembrance of <s>Viṣṇu</s>.
Thereafter he should set out, accompanied by the four-limbed army.
Auspicious is the blessed <s>Viṣṇu</s>; auspicious is he whose banner bears <s>Garuḍa</s>.
Auspicious is the lotus-eyed one; <s>Hari</s> is the abode of auspiciousness.
Gain is theirs, victory is theirs; whence could defeat be theirs,
for those in whose heart <s>Janārdana</s>, dark as a blue lotus, is established?
<s>Arjuna</s>, <s>Phālguna</s>, <s>Jiṣṇu</s>, the diademed one, the white-horsed one,
<s>Bībhatsu</s>, <s>Vijaya</s>, <s>Kṛṣṇa</s>, <s>Savyasācī</s>, and <s>Dhanañjaya</s>:
a man, intent and purified, should remember these names of <s>Arjuna</s>.
An <s>akṣauhiṇī</s> is held to be two kha-units, with gods, wealth, moon, and eyes as numerals.
And the <s>akṣauhiṇī</s> is prescribed as consisting of armored chariots.
Those who know the principles of numerical reckoning say there are twenty-one thousand,
with eight hundreds above, and also seventy, O king.
The measure of elephants too should be specified as just the same.
Sixty-five thousand, six hundred, with ten added above:

children.text: hayāṇāṃ ca parimāṇam etad eva suniścitam
children.translated_text: this measure of horses is likewise definitely settled.

children.text: jñeyaṃ lakṣaṃ padātīnāṃ sahasrāṇi tathā nava ||
children.translated_text: The infantry should be known as one lakh, and likewise nine thousand,
three hundred and fifty brave weapon-bearing men.
And of horses there are sixty-five thousand, with hundreds as well,
with ten added, so people who know the truth of numbers recite.
A great <s>akṣauhiṇī</s> should be made; its chariot-warriors are remembered as a crore.
Thirty-seven lakhs are recited by those who know the truth,
and exactly twelve thousand, as well as four hundred.
Ninety are stated in the same way; thus elephants too are understood.
The horses are measured as four crores, and also eleven lakhs,
thirty-seven thousand, and likewise four hundred,
and with seven; the foot-soldiers too are declared to be counted thus.
Six crores, eighty lakhs, and five more hundreds,
sixty-two thousand, and likewise four hundred.

children.text: agre rathā gajāḥ pṛṣṭhe tatpṛṣṭhe ca padātayaḥ
children.translated_text: Chariots should be in front, elephants behind, and infantry behind them.
Horses should be placed on the two flanks; this is remembered as the rule for the number of the battle array.

children.text: ardhacandraṃ ca candraṃ ca śakaṭaṃ makaraṃ tathā
children.translated_text: The half-moon, the moon, the cart, and the makara,

children.text: kamalaṃ śreṇikāṃ gulmaṃ vyūhān evaṃ prakalpate ||
children.translated_text: the lotus, the line, and the troop-cluster: thus one should arrange the battle formations.
Those princes, feudatories, trusted men, and classes of servants
who always act for one's welfare should be carefully protected.

children.text: yasmin raṇe yaḥ puruṣaḥ pradhānaḥ sa sarvayatnena hi rakṣaṇīyaḥ
children.translated_text: In whatever battle a man is foremost, he must indeed be protected with every effort.

children.text: tasmin vinaṣṭe kila sarvabhūte sarve'pi yodhāstvabalā bhavanti ||
children.translated_text: For when he is lost, all the beings, all the warriors too, become powerless.
If one has at command a knower of śāstra who is the very essence of battle,

children.text: api ca svaśriyai sainyaṃ vṛtheyaṃ muṇḍamaṇḍalī ||
children.translated_text: then even for one's own fortune this army is otherwise a useless circle of shaved heads.

children.text: api pañcaśatāḥ śūrā gṛhṇanti mahatīṃ camūm
children.translated_text: Even five hundred heroes can seize a great army,
or else five, six, or seven obedient followers can win victory.
Kings whose bows are well joined and whose selves are purified are weak in speech;
warriors grey-haired up to the ears speak of victory in battle.
Warriors who are mutually attached, bearing <s>Śārṅga</s>-like bows,
and skilled in war, mounted on chariots, conquer enemies in battle.
One man, broken by cowardice, may split apart a great army.
When that has been split, even the bravest warriors split apart after it.
And by being hard to restrain, he may terrify an entire great army,
like a great torrent of waters, even if they are skilled.
Even when armies are broken and have fled, if one turns back,
at every step he obtains the imperishable fruit of the horse sacrifice.
There are these two men in the world who pierce the disk of the sun:
the wandering ascetic joined to yoga, and one killed while facing battle.

children.text: yatra yatra hataḥ śūraḥ śatrubhiḥ pariveṣṭitaḥ
children.translated_text: Wherever a hero is killed, surrounded by enemies,

children.text: akṣayaṃ labhate lokaṃ yadi dainyaṃ na bhāṣate ||
children.translated_text: he obtains an imperishable world, provided he does not speak words of dejection.
One should not kill someone fainted, disabled, without a weapon, or fighting another,

children.text: palāyamāṇaṃ śaraṇaṃ gataṃ caiva na hiṃsayet ||
children.translated_text: nor one who is fleeing or who has gone for refuge.
Even a coward who is fleeing should not be killed by a stronger man.
At some time he may attain heroism, forgetting that refuge has been granted.
Having duly honored the great four-limbed army, the king
should arrange it in formation and station the enemy's heroes, desiring victory.

children.text: alpāyāṃ vā mahatyāṃ vā senāyāmiti niścayaḥ
children.translated_text: Whether the army is small or great, this is the settled conclusion:
the joy of the body of warriors too is called a mark of victory.

children.text: anvevaṃ vāyavo yānti dakṣiṇe ca vayāṃsi ca
children.translated_text: When the winds go following after in this way, and birds on the right,

children.text: anusarve'pi piśitā yasya yānti raṇe jayaḥ ||
children.translated_text: and all flesh-eaters also go after someone, victory in battle is his.
What is incomplete should be regarded as succeeding only through what is complete.
Therefore courage must be practiced; the enemy army must be struck down.
While living there is fortune; when dead, heaven; and fame on the surface of the earth.
Therefore courage must be established; the enemy army must be struck down.
Thus ends the <s>Dhanurveda</s> spoken by the illustrious <s>Sadāśiva</s>.
